hints: Start from the beam numbers: average current $1.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A}$ for time $3.0 \text{ s}$ - what total charge $Q = I t$ arrives at the target?
Recall what charge one $\alpha$-particle carries in vacuum: a helium nucleus with 2 protons, so $q = +2e$ where $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Connect the two with $Q = N q$, so $N = I t / (2e)$ - check why dividing by $e$ alone would double the count.
walkthrough: Identify the delivered charge from current and time: $I = Q/t$, so $Q = I t$.
Substitute values with units: $Q = (1.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A})(3.0 \text{ s}) = 4.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$.
State the charge per $\alpha$-particle: an $\alpha$-particle is a $^4_2\text{He}$ nucleus, so $q = 2e = 2(1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}) = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Set up the particle count: total charge $Q = N q$, so $N = Q/q = (4.5 \times 10^{-9})/(3.2 \times 10^{-19})$.
Calculate and check units: $N \approx 1.41 \times 10^{10}$ with no unit, as charge divided by charge per particle. This is option C.

options.A: Gives only about one-third of the required particles, as $N \times 2e$ would be about $1.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$ and not the full $I t$ charge for $3.0 \text{ s}$.
options.B: Gives about two-thirds of the required particles, as $N \times 2e$ would be about $3.0 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$ which is less than $I t = 4.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$.
options.C: Gives $Q = I t = 4.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$ divided by the alpha charge $2e = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, equal to about $1.4 \times 10^{10}$ particles.
options.D: Equals $Q/e$ with $Q = 4.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$, so it forgets that an $\alpha$-particle has charge $+2e$ and counts twice too many particles.
